limitations: The analysed patients were a subset who underwent resection for symptoms, concern about malignancy or lack of a definitive diagnosis, so their characteristics may differ from an unselected population and the results may not apply to all patients with a pancreatic cyst
The CEA results, and particularly the cutoff values, may not be applicable if CEA assays with different characteristics are used
critique: The 192 ng/mL threshold was selected to maximise correct classification in the same 112 patients in which it was then tested, with no split-sample, cross-validation or external cohort, so 79% accuracy is an optimistic in-sample estimate and the figure that entered every subsequent guideline was never validated here

Only 112 of 341 enrolled patients (33%) had histological verification, and verification depended on the very findings under test - a worrying EUS appearance or suspicious cytology made resection more likely - which is partial verification bias and distorts the apparent performance of all three tests in directions that cannot be signed from the data given

Mucinous lesions were 60% of the verified cohort and 59% of those were malignant or borderline, far above community prevalence, so the predictive values implied by these sensitivities and specificities do not transport to an incidental cyst clinic

Cytology was read by local cytologists at each of 13 institutions with no central review, while CEA was assayed centrally and blindly; the comparison therefore pits a standardised test against an unstandardised one, which penalises cytology by design

Cyst fluid was explicitly not analysed for amylase, mucin concentration or viscosity, so the comparison omits the cheapest and most widely used discriminators, including the one test that reliably excludes a pseudocyst

Only 7 serous cystadenomas were verified, so the low-CEA half of the claim rests on single digits, and the inflammatory group (n=27) carries a mean CEA of 36.8 ng/mL, which means the test's specificity for mucinous disease is being established largely against pseudocysts rather than against serous lesions

The study's conclusion - that endoscopists should send aspirated fluid for CEA - rests on a marker the data show cannot distinguish benign from malignant mucinous disease, since CEA ranges overlapped widely within the malignant group; the clinical decision that matters is left unaddressed
Histological interpretation was done locally and only reviewed from reports by one study pathologist, not from slides, so the reference standard itself was not uniformly applied
15131794.n: 341 consecutive patients enrolled and underwent EUS-FNA; 112 with histological confirmation analysed (68 mucinous, 7 serous, 27 inflammatory, 5 endocrine, 5 other)
15131794.bottom_line: The study that established cyst fluid CEA at 192 ng/mL as the most accurate single test for separating mucinous from non-mucinous pancreatic cysts, at about 80% accuracy and better than EUS morphology or cytology either alone or combined; it does not establish that CEA identifies which mucinous cysts harbour high-grade dysplasia or cancer, and its threshold was derived and tested in the same 112-patient surgical subset.

limitations: Wide variation in cytology sensitivity between studies, probably reflecting differences in cytopathologist experience, so sensitivity and specificity may be lower in non-specialised centres where aspirates are rarely seen

Rare cystic neoplasms including IPMT, pseudopapillary and solid tumours, cystic islet-cell tumours, lymphangioma, sarcoma and benign cysts - together 10-25% of all pancreatic cystic tumours - were excluded, so the data cannot be applied to them
Too few studies existed to pool other markers or viscosity, and there may be no added benefit from them over amylase, CEA and cytology
No multiple-regression analysis was performed to validate the suggestion that CEA, amylase, cytology and CA19-9 each have independent value in different subsets
critique: The cutoffs were chosen to maximise correct classification within the same pooled dataset in which they are then reported, and the CEA >800 ng/mL threshold is described as 'arbitrarily set'; there is no validation sample, so all the operating characteristics are in-sample

The 450-patient figure is not a cohort: each marker has a different and much smaller denominator (amylase 155, CA19-9 136), the contributing studies did not all measure all markers, and so the apparent mutual consistency of the markers is partly determined by which studies happened to report which assay

The reference standard is not uniform or symmetric: nearly all MCA and MCAC were confirmed histologically or cytologically, whereas in two studies pseudocysts were diagnosed from a pancreatitis history plus follow-up and many SCAs were unverified - differential verification of the malignant arm inflates specificity for mucinous disease

The Frossard data were excluded post hoc because SCA CEA values were discordantly high, with no pre-specified rule and no explanation found; the authors report both versions, which is honest, but the headline numbers are the ones that survive the exclusion
Individual values were read off published scatter grams rather than obtained from authors, so extraction error is unquantified and unquantifiable

The analysis predates and explicitly excludes IPMN, which is now the commonest neoplastic pancreatic cyst; the management table the paper proposes - resect on CEA >800 or malignant cytology, do not resect on CEA <5 or CA19-9 <37 - therefore cannot be applied to the modal patient in current practice, and the omission is noted only as a caveat about rare tumours

Every cutoff has a sensitivity at or below 50%, so all four tests are rule-in only; the paper nonetheless advises 'no resection needed' on the strength of CEA <5 ng/mL and CA19-9 <37 U/mL, whose negative predictive values are 55% and 38% in its own tables
CA19-9 is recommended as an adjunct for indeterminate CEA on the basis of 136 patients and an accuracy of 46%, which is barely better than chance in a cohort with roughly even group sizes
16111956.n: 12 studies, 450 patients; amylase available in 155 (60 pseudocyst, 32 SCA, 32 MCA, 31 MCAC), CEA in 332 (125/79/64/64), CA19-9 in 136 (66/24/24/22), cytology for malignancy in 111
16111956.bottom_line: Pooled individual-patient data fix the specificity of amylase <250 U/L, CEA <5 ng/mL, CEA >800 ng/mL and CA19-9 <37 U/mL at 95-98% with sensitivities of 19-50%, making each a rule-in rather than a screening test, and put cytology's sensitivity for malignancy at 48%; it establishes nothing about IPMN, which was excluded, and all its cutoffs were fitted to the data that report them.

limitations: The guidelines are explicitly provisional - the authors state they represent the working group's consensus 'at this moment' and that as understanding grows they will need revision
Considerable gaps are acknowledged in knowledge of the natural history of these neoplasms, with 'practically no information' on the natural history of branch-duct IPMN
Data on the prevalence of invasive carcinoma in MCN are hard to interpret because few studies used ovarian-type stroma as a necessary criterion
More data from pathological studies of branch-duct IPMN over 30 mm without main duct dilation or mural nodules are needed to determine whether all such lesions should be resected immediately
The interval between follow-up examinations 'remains to be determined', and there is no evidence in the literature to define the frequency or type of surveillance required after resection
Frozen-section grading of IPMN is subjective and frozen tissue artefacts compound the difficulty; denuded epithelium frequently makes margin assessment impossible
It is impossible to diagnose minimally invasive carcinoma derived from IPMN or MCN preoperatively
The relative risk and biologic significance of the various grades and subsets of IPMN have not been fully established
critique: There is no cohort - n is null - and every malignancy rate quoted, from 70% for main-duct IPMN to 25% for branch-duct and 6-36% for MCN, is the prevalence of malignancy in resected specimens, that is in cysts selected for operation; the document applies these figures to management decisions about unresected lesions without any correction for that selection, and the arithmetic of what fraction of all such cysts they represent is never attempted

The series behind the tables are small and heterogeneous (12-140 patients, with 8 of 9 main-duct series under 50), and the 'mean of all series' is an unweighted average across studies with different definitions of malignancy, different eras and different inclusion of asymptomatic patients; the authors themselves observe that the two branch-duct series with 30-31% invasive cancer contained no asymptomatic patients, which explains the entire spread and undercuts pooling a mean at all

No evidence grading, no systematic search and no account of how consensus was reached or whether it was unanimous; the thresholds that became the Sendai criteria - 30 mm, mural nodules, main duct >6 mm, symptoms - derive from univariate and multivariate analyses in two Japanese series of 15-32 patients

The recommendation to resect all main-duct and mixed IPMN was made with no data at all on what happens to unresected main-duct IPMN, and is justified in part by inference - that 'clonal progression' and the age difference between benign and malignant cases indicate most benign main-duct lesions will progress - rather than by observation

The recommendation to resect all MCNs rests on malignancy rates from series that largely did not require ovarian stroma, which the text concedes inflates them, and on the assertion that left pancreatectomy carries 'low morbidity and practically no mortality' with no pooled estimate; the risk side of every resection recommendation in the document is unquantified

The 30 mm and 6 mm thresholds that trigger resection on follow-up are the same numbers used to define a low-risk lesion at baseline, with no evidence that a lesion crossing them during observation carries the same risk as one presenting with them
No end point to surveillance is offered, no cost consideration enters, and no competing-risk framing is applied despite an explicitly elderly branch-duct population in the sixth and seventh decades
The working group that wrote the criteria largely comprises the authors of the series on which the criteria are based, and the document records no external review or validation plan
16327281.bottom_line: The first international consensus on IPMN and MCN, which fixed the vocabulary - main-duct versus branch-duct, ovarian-type stroma as a requirement for MCN - and introduced the resection thresholds later known as the Sendai criteria; it establishes none of them empirically, since the guideline has no cohort, all its malignancy rates are prevalences in small resected series, and no data on the natural history of unresected lesions existed when it was written.

limitations: The levels of evidence for all items addressed are low, being 4 or 5, so the authors designate these 'consensus' rather than 'evidence-based' guidelines; grades of recommendation are so low that grade C has been omitted from almost all items as repetitive
The vast majority of the data are retrospective and uncontrolled with limited long-term follow-up, so knowledge of the natural history is still incomplete

Differences in the proportions of each IPMN type and in malignancy risk are partly caused by variation in type definitions, since the correlation between histologic and radiologic criteria is only around 70%

Whether the surveillance interval can be lengthened after 2 years of no change is controversial, with some authors advocating continued 6-monthly surveillance because of the relatively high incidence of PDAC in branch-duct IPMN

Cyst fluid analysis is still investigational, and interpreting biochemical markers is a complex exercise in pattern recognition that should be reserved for patients in whom the information will affect surgical decision-making
It is unclear whether a microscopically positive margin for moderately dysplastic IPMN increases recurrence, and there is little evidence to guide the frequency or type of postoperative surveillance

Recurrence rates after resection are difficult to determine because main duct dilation in the remnant may be secondary to anastomotic stenosis, and better postoperative imaging may reveal previously undetected IPMN
The relationship between a rapid growth rate and malignancy risk remains unclear
critique: n is null - the guideline has no cohort - and the pooled malignancy figures that justify the new risk framework come from 3568 resected IPMNs, so they describe the yield of past operating decisions rather than the risk faced by a surveilled patient; the table itself carries '>' signs because some contributing series reported only invasive cases, meaning numerators and denominators are not consistently defined across the pool

The central change, lowering the main-duct threshold from 10 mm to more than 5 mm, cites references for improved sensitivity but no study comparing outcomes above and below the new line; the same document then classifies 5-9 mm as a worrisome feature not warranting resection, so a duct can define main-duct disease and simultaneously be observed, and the resulting expansion of the 'mixed type' category is noted as a classification problem but its consequences for management are not addressed

The 2-3% annual malignancy rate in observed branch-duct IPMN and the 25.5% resected malignancy rate are placed on facing pages without reconciling that they are incompatible estimates of the same underlying quantity

High-risk stigmata and worrisome features were assembled from univariate associations in surgical series; no multivariable model, no validation cohort and no operating characteristics - sensitivity, specificity, predictive values - are reported for either tier, so a clinician cannot know what a 'worrisome feature' actually predicts

The recommendation to resect every MCN in a fit patient appears two sentences after the statement that ovarian-stroma-defined MCN has under 15% invasive carcinoma and no malignancy below 4 cm without mural nodules; the guidance is more aggressive than the evidence it cites, and the justification shifts to the cost of years of high-resolution imaging rather than to risk

Surgical mortality and morbidity are nowhere quantified in the document, so every resection recommendation is presented one-sidedly, with the risk of the alternative stated numerically and the risk of the intervention not stated at all

The Japanese objection to EUS-FNA of any cyst with worrisome features is recorded as a regional belief supported by two case-level citations, which leaves the single most informative preoperative test governed by geography rather than data and makes the cytology-based criteria unobtainable in much of the world

No stopping rule is offered, no cost analysis is attempted and no competing-risk framing is applied to a disease of the sixth and seventh decades, even though the document's own argument for observing branch-duct IPMN rests on patients being elderly

Fourteen authors, most of whom authored the series pooled in the evidence table, and no declaration of how disagreements were resolved, whether consensus was unanimous, or what conflicts of interest existed
22687371.bottom_line: The Fukuoka revision that created the high-risk-stigmata and worrisome-features framework still in use, lowered the main-duct threshold to more than 5 mm, replaced carcinoma in situ with high-grade dysplasia, substaged T1, and moved branch-duct IPMN over 3 cm from resection to observation; by the authors' own account every recommendation rests on level 4-5 evidence, the two risk tiers have no reported operating characteristics, and the malignancy rates behind them are prevalences in resected specimens.

limitations: The study explicitly does not reach the level of evidence needed to make recommendations on the type and timing of follow-up
Features of recurrent IPMN in terms of invasion were defined through radiology and cytology for patients who were not reoperated
12 of 412 resections could not be pathologically reclassified and 8 patients were lost to follow-up
The authors cannot rule out that the small branch-duct lesions left in the remnant harboured high-grade dysplasia
critique: 'Recurrence' is defined as the radiologic appearance of a new IPMN, with growth of knowingly retained lesions excluded by definition; the central distinction between true recurrence, progression of residual disease and a field defect is therefore settled by the definition rather than by evidence, and most recurrences were never histologically confirmed

The hazard ratio of 20.9 for high-grade dysplasia at the margin derives from 10 margin-positive patients and a handful of events, is reported with a P value of .03 and no confidence interval, and should not be carried into practice as an effect size

The headline contrast between non-invasive main-duct IPMN recurring as invasive cancer in 83% and branch-duct in 5% rests on 6 and 22 events, and the much-quoted '1 of 197' figure is a single patient; neither supports the inference that follow-up after benign branch-duct resection can be omitted

Follow-up intensity differed by design between groups - 6-monthly for the first 3 years in invasive IPMN versus annually then every 2-3 years for non-invasive - so the later median recurrence of benign lesions (52 vs 19 months) is partly a detection interval, and the paper treats it as a biological difference

The 0.5% metachronous PDAC rate is the paper's strongest claim against the field-defect concern and against the Japanese literature, but 19 concomitant PDACs were excluded from the recurrence cohort beforehand, and the comparison with the expected rate in this age group is asserted by citation rather than computed as a standardised incidence ratio

Accrual spans 23 years, across which imaging resolution, the WHO grading system, the epithelial subtype classification and surveillance practice all changed; the single-pathologist re-review standardises the pathology but cannot standardise the surveillance that generated the recurrence endpoint

The conclusion that follow-up after resection of a benign branch-duct IPMN 'could be avoided' in older individuals is an extrapolation from a cohort with a median 58-month follow-up to a decision with lifelong consequences, and sits against the paper's own observation that oncocytic lesions recurred as late as 11 years

Recurrence after middle pancreatectomy (22%) is three times that after Whipple or distal resection, which could reflect either the operation or the selection of patients for it; no adjustment is attempted and the finding is reported without a causal caveat
25793719.n: 412 resected IPMNs; 400 available for pathological reclassification (176 main duct, 224 branch duct including 50 'minimal main' mixed); 381 available for recurrence analysis after excluding 19 with concomitant PDAC; 288 survivors followed a median 58 months (range 3-236), with only 8 lost to follow-up (98% complete data)
25793719.bottom_line: The largest and longest-followed resected-IPMN series establishes that recurrence occurs in 17% and depends on the invasive component (45% vs 9%), margin status and histologic subtype, that non-invasive branch-duct lesions essentially never recur as cancer, and that small branch-duct lesions deliberately left in the remnant can be watched safely; it does not establish a surveillance schedule, and its key subgroup claims rest on single-digit event counts.
25793719.funding: No funding statement; the authors declare no conflicts of interest

limitations: All the evidence related to the management of pancreatic cysts is graded as very low quality; nearly all data derive from case series, often retrospective, with major unexplained heterogeneity between studies, and they did not directly evaluate reduced mortality from pancreatic adenocarcinoma as the key outcome

The authors state that a reasonable argument can be advanced that no recommendations regarding management can be made at all because the evidence is so conditional, and that it is unclear whether the benefits of surveillance outweigh the risks for most patients
The 1-year then 2-yearly surveillance interval is explicitly not based on any evidence
No statistically significant association was found between a dilated pancreatic duct and malignancy in the review of unselected cysts, yet it was included as a high-risk factor
There are no data on the impact of multiple high-risk features on the risk of malignancy
No data specifically compare rates of cancer in stable cysts versus cysts that change over time
There have been no dedicated cost-effectiveness analyses of surveillance of incidental pancreatic cysts
It is unclear how many cases of high-grade dysplasia would have progressed to invasive malignancy, so the proportion of patients who truly benefit from surgery is unclear even in the high-risk group
The estimate of 28% 5-year survival after resection of invasive cancer may be prone to lead-time and length-time bias, which if present would further reduce any surgical benefit
No evidence was identified at all to support post-resection MRI surveillance, and no case series report outcomes after resection of a cyst without high-grade dysplasia
The guideline anticipates significant controversy because it advocates less frequent follow-up and a higher threshold before offering EUS or surgery
critique: n is null and the guideline sets two incommensurable evidence streams against each other without resolving them: a 0.25% prevalence of malignancy and a 0.24% per year conversion rate, both derived by assuming that every pancreatic cancer arises in a cyst and dividing SEER incidence by an estimated cyst population, versus a 15% malignancy rate in resected series. The first is a denominator-inflated population estimate and the second a selection-inflated surgical one, and the stopping rule - the guideline's most consequential recommendation - is built entirely on the first

Requiring two of three high-risk features for EUS-FNA, and both a solid component and a dilated duct for surgery, is an explicit claim about joint test performance, yet the guideline states there are no data on multiple features and asserts additivity by analogy; the estimated specificity of over 95% for that combination is a guess, and Singhi and Lekkerkerker subsequently measured 79% specificity with a 38-45% miss rate and a 12% miss rate for high-grade dysplasia or cancer respectively

A dilated main pancreatic duct was retained as a high-risk feature after the guideline's own systematic review of unselected cysts found no significant association, on the basis of resected IPMN series - precisely the selection-biased reasoning the document criticises elsewhere, and it is one of only three features on which the entire algorithm turns

Scope is restricted to asymptomatic cysts and explicitly excludes main-duct IPMN without side-branch involvement, so the lesion with the highest malignancy rate falls outside the guidance, while the case series on which the recommendations rest included symptomatic patients in a large proportion of their cohorts - a mismatch between the evidence and the population the guideline governs

Recommendation 10 - no surveillance after resection of a cyst without high-grade dysplasia or malignancy - is conceded to rest on no case series at all, and it depends on a field-defect argument the guideline asserts in the opposite direction one recommendation earlier; the two statements cannot both follow from the evidence presented

The stopping rule at 5 years and the 2-yearly interval constitute a population-level trade-off that is never stated as such: no absolute number of cancers expected to be missed is calculated, no cost-effectiveness analysis is offered despite cost being given as a central justification, and the consequences for the individual patient are left to the opening ungraded statement about understanding risks and benefits

Applying the GRADE apparatus to a body of evidence the authors themselves grade as very low throughout confers a formal precision the inputs cannot support; GRADE is designed to separate strong from weak evidence, and here it returns 'very low' for all ten statements, which means the method is distinguishing nothing

The guideline advises surgery only when specificity is likely high, in order to avoid operating on benign disease, while acknowledging that the surgery it would then permit has 2% mortality and 30% major morbidity in centres of excellence and 6.6% mortality nationally; the asymmetry between the precision demanded of the diagnostic threshold and the imprecision tolerated in the surgical risk estimate is never examined
25805375.bottom_line: The first guideline to set an explicit stopping rule - no further surveillance after 5 years of stability or once a patient is unfit for surgery - and to raise the threshold for EUS-FNA and surgery to two or more high-risk features; by its own GRADE assessment every recommendation rests on very low quality evidence, the surveillance intervals are stated to be unsupported by any evidence, a dilated duct was retained as a risk factor despite showing no significant association, and the stopping rule rests on a population-level annual transformation estimate of 0.24% with no data comparing stable with changing cysts.

limitations: The method of recruitment and the way data were recorded are open to criticism
No central review of imaging studies or pathology specimens
Cyst measurements could not be guaranteed uniform across centres
Follow-up was short, although similar to other studies except one
Surgical morbidity was not recorded because the study was retrospective
Growth rate interpretation is limited by short follow-up and only two imaging time points, and assumes linear rather than curvilinear growth
Operative mortality was much lower than reported for high-volume centres (1-3%) and was probably underestimated in this self-reporting study
No conclusion was drawn about the prevalence of locally aggressive SCN because definitions differed between centres
critique: The operated and non-operated groups are not exchangeable: G1 cysts were significantly larger (40 vs 25 mm) and more often symptomatic (52% vs 23%), so the benign natural history described here is read off precisely the cysts that were selected against resection

The headline claim that disease-specific mortality is 'almost nil' uses a denominator of 1032 non-operated patients, which by construction excludes every patient whose cyst worried a clinician enough to operate; the whole-cohort figure is not given

785 patients (30%) had a radiological diagnosis only, and the paper itself reports blinded CT and MRI accuracy for SCN as low as 27%, so an unknown fraction of the SCN denominator were other cyst types - including mucinous lesions, which would both dilute the benign picture and misattribute any malignancy

The 0.1% malignancy rate counts only distant metastasis beyond the peripancreatic bed, per WHO; 18 locally aggressive lesions with vascular, nodal or perineural involvement are set aside, so the figure is a definitional artefact as much as a biological one

Operative mortality, the risk side of the risk-benefit comparison the paper draws, is self-reported and acknowledged to be lower than high-volume-centre estimates, so the comparison is biased toward conservative management by a mechanism the authors name but do not correct
Two of the three cystadenocarcinoma patients were lost to follow-up (at 1 and 9 years), so survival after malignant SCN is described as indolent on the basis of a single patient followed one year

Follow-up starts at the first imaging on which the cyst was seen, which for a lesion often present for years is an arbitrary origin, and no competing-risk framing is applied in a cohort with a median age of 58 and 30% with other cancers
Some recruited patients had already been published in series from the participating centres, so the cohort is not independent of the prior literature it supersedes
26045140.n: 2622 patients from 23 countries and 71 centres; 1351 operated within 1 year (G1), 239 operated after 1 year (G2), 1032 non-operated (G3)
26045140.bottom_line: The largest SCN series ever assembled shows the lesion is almost always benign, grows slowly, rarely becomes symptomatic and essentially never kills, supporting conservative management; it does not establish the true malignancy rate or long-term outcome, because 61% of the cohort was resected, nearly a third of diagnoses were radiological only, and median follow-up was about 3 years.
26045140.funding: No funding statement; competing interests declared were that AM Lennon is a consultant for Boston Scientific and P Levy for AbbVie and Mayoly Spindler

limitations: Retrospective by design, and it did not adhere to the algorithm in the AGA clinical decision support tool - all patients were evaluated from EUS-FNA data rather than abdominal MRI, and since EUS-FNA is significantly more sensitive than MRI for malignancy, the observed 62% sensitivity should be considered an overestimate of the AGA rule's real performance
Including patients referred for EUS-FNA introduces an inherent selection bias toward those more likely to have advanced neoplasia

Diagnostic pathology was unavailable for most of the cohort, although the aim was only short-term sensitivity and specificity, and obtaining diagnostic material for a large cohort within the timeframe is not feasible since most cysts are non-neoplastic or benign

The study includes both asymptomatic and symptomatic patients whereas the AGA guidelines pertain only to asymptomatic neoplastic cysts, which the authors argue is itself a flawed restriction since 7 of the 9 studies in the AGA technical review documented symptoms in 46-74% of their cohorts

The alternative approach was developed retrospectively in a patient cohort limited in size and requires prospective, independent validation in a larger population with corresponding diagnostic pathology; additional criteria or changes may prove necessary
The selection of a 1.5 cm cyst size threshold is certainly debatable and the supporting evidence is admittedly weak
critique: Every performance figure rests on 41 verified patients and 13 events, so the headline 62% sensitivity is 8 of 13; no confidence intervals are reported anywhere, and an interval around that proportion would be wide enough to include both the AGA's claimed specificity of over 95% and performance considerably worse than observed

The alternative algorithm was constructed by inspecting these same 41 cases and is then scored on them, which is why it attains 100% sensitivity and 100% NPV; a fitted model is presented in direct numerical comparison with an externally specified rule, and the paper's framing invites the reader to treat the two as commensurable
The molecular sensitivities described as 100% come from 23 resected IPMNs and 2 serous cystadenomas, and the TP53/PIK3CA/PTEN figure of 91% sensitivity is 10 of 11

A second structural asymmetry goes unnamed: the AGA rule is applied as a surgical trigger while the authors' pathway is scored as a referral-and-surveillance trigger, with cases routed to 'Surveillance Plan A with consideration for surgery' counted as correctly identified - the two schemes are being asked different questions and graded on different outcomes

The cost argument is one-sided: the $211,491 for SCA surveillance under the AGA rule is calculated, but the cost of the additional EUS-FNAs generated by lowering the referral threshold from 3 cm to 1.5 cm is acknowledged to increase and never priced, nor is the cost of the molecular panel for the whole cohort

Excluding main-duct IPMN from the cohort removes the lesions with the highest malignancy rate, so the test characteristics do not describe the population any guideline must serve, and the AGA guideline's own exclusion of main-duct disease is criticised while the study replicates it

The molecular panel is the authors' own clinical assay, performed in their own laboratory and promoted in the proposed pathway; the only declared support is a National Pancreas Foundation grant to the senior author, who is also the pathologist adjudicating the reference standard

The verified subset had an advanced neoplasia prevalence of 32% versus 6% in the whole cohort, so the predictive values reported for both the AGA criteria and the alternative pathway are computed in a population roughly five times enriched for the outcome
26709110.n: 225 patients who underwent EUS-FNA for a pancreatic cyst (age 16-89, mean 64.7, median 67; 56% female); diagnostic pathology available for 41 (18%), of whom 13 (32% of those verified, 6% of the cohort) had advanced neoplasia
26709110.bottom_line: Shows that applying the 2015 AGA criteria to a consecutive EUS-FNA cohort misses 38% of cysts with advanced neoplasia and 45% of IPMNs with high-grade dysplasia or cancer while sending 43% of the patients it selects to unnecessary surgery, and that patients with serous cystadenomas would be surveilled indefinitely; the counts are small (13 events in 41 verified patients, no confidence intervals), main-duct IPMN was excluded, and the superior molecular algorithm was derived and scored in the same cases.
26709110.funding: Dr Singhi received research support in part for this study from a grant from the National Pancreas Foundation, Western Pennsylvania Chapter; all other authors disclosed no financial relationships relevant to the publication

limitations: Most patients had a presumptive rather than definitive diagnosis, since EUS with FNA was performed in only 35%, and errors in the preoperative diagnosis of pancreatic cystic tumours are common - particularly for the branch-duct IPMNs that made up 57% of the cohort
Retrospective design
Median follow-up was under 5 years, so no definitive conclusion about the real risk of progression in patients with worrisome features can be drawn; only longer follow-up will answer this

The cohort is a selected group because most patients, especially those with high-risk stigmata, avoided surgery because of advanced age and comorbidities, so the conclusions may not apply to younger patients or to those with a strong family history of pancreatic cancer

Enhancing nodules were identified in only 22 patients (8%) and any nodules in 48 (17%), and the presence of nodules may have prompted clinicians to operate without delay, so the failure to identify nodules as an independent predictor should be interpreted cautiously
The study did not analyse the timing or modality of IPMN progression or predictors of progression
critique: The cut-offs of 70 years, 50 mm and 15 mm were chosen by dichotomising the cohort at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles and selecting the split that maximised the log-rank chi-square - in the same patients in which the resulting hazard ratios are reported; the MPD >15 mm hazard ratio of 9.6 is therefore an optimised in-sample threshold presented in the same table as guideline cut-offs that were not optimised

The multivariable models carry fifteen to twenty covariates against 25 IPMN-related deaths and produce confidence intervals such as 2.94-156.72 and 3.73-216.36; these are not interpretable effect sizes, and in that data regime the surviving 'independent predictors' are largely artefacts of sparse-data bias rather than findings

Disease-specific survival is the wrong denominator for a decision about surgery in a cohort with a median age of 70 and an ACE-27 of 2 or 3 in half the patients: 32 of 57 deaths were from other causes, competing risk is invoked rhetorically but the Kaplan-Meier estimates ignore it, so the 96.2% five-year DSS systematically overstates the benefit of avoiding surgery

38 patients (13.5%) crossed over to surgery and 36 were resected, 10 of them with high-grade dysplasia or invasive carcinoma, yet all are kept in the non-operative analysis on the grounds that surgery did not affect survival; the 96.2% DSS for worrisome features is therefore a property of a cohort partly rescued by resection, not of observation alone

Postoperative mortality among the 36 resected patients was 8% - three deaths, all in patients whose final pathology showed non-invasive IPMN - and this is reported in a single clause without comment, although it is the central number for any reader weighing the alternative the paper is recommending against

Only 35% had cytology, yet atypical and malignant cytology are two of the five independent DSS predictors and rest on 11 and 5 patients respectively; a predictor measured in a third of the cohort cannot be compared on equal terms with imaging features measured in all of it

Progression occurred in 52% of patients at a median of 32 months while median follow-up was 51 months, so for a substantial fraction of the cohort the observation window barely exceeded the time to progression; 'low progression' in the title describes progression to invasive cancer (12%), not progression of the lesion (52%)

Three of the six contributing centres are the groups that wrote the ICG-II criteria being evaluated here, and 91 patients (32.5%) entered the non-operative cohort on physician recommendation - that is, because the authors' own colleagues judged them low risk, which is the outcome under test
26743012.n: 281 patients (58% male, median age 70, range 33-89): 159 (57%) branch-duct IPMN and 122 (43%) main-duct or mixed (99 mixed, 23 main duct only); 231 (82%) with worrisome features and 50 (18%) with high-risk stigmata
26743012.bottom_line: The largest series of IPMN with worrisome features or high-risk stigmata managed without surgery, establishing a roughly tenfold difference in IPMN-related death between the two tiers (5-year disease-specific survival 96.2% vs 60.2%) and so supporting the Fukuoka division and observation of worrisome features in elderly comorbid patients; it does not establish long-term safety, because median follow-up was 51 months, 13.5% crossed over to surgery, competing risks are ignored and the cohort was selected for being unfit or unwilling.
26743012.funding: No funding statement; competing interests none declared; the retrospective study was approved by the Internal Review Board

limitations: It cannot be predicted whether the resected non-malignant cysts would have progressed if left alone, particularly those with low-grade and borderline dysplasia, where it is unknown whether and when progression would occur
The 10 mm definition of cyst growth is arbitrary; change in size should always be considered in the context of the original cyst size and the interval between images

Selection bias: only patients who underwent resection were evaluated, so the number of patients in the surveillance cohort who warranted resection because of high-grade dysplasia is actually unknown, and this bias is inevitable because definitive diagnosis and grading require histopathology
The number of false-negative preoperative diagnoses of 'innocent' cysts is therefore unknown and could not be compared between the guidelines
No single standardised treatment protocol was applied; decisions rested on the consensus of the multidisciplinary pancreatic meeting, generally following the IAP and European guidelines
critique: The design can measure only one side of each guideline's error: among patients already resected it can count unnecessary operations and retrospectively missed cancers, but it cannot count the cancers a guideline would have missed in patients never operated on, so the reported sensitivities are conditional on resection and the between-guideline comparison is not a comparison of accuracy

The cohort was managed by the IAP and European guidelines, which therefore determined who entered the denominator; this guarantees that those two guidelines appear to miss nothing, while the AGA criteria - applied retrospectively to a population they never selected - appear to miss cases. The structure of the study produces its headline result

The '12% missed' figure is 4 patients, and the descriptions make clear that the same two lesions (a 15 mm main-duct IPMN and a 2.3 cm side-branch IPMN with a nodule) are counted once as malignant and once as high-grade dysplasia, so the finding rests on two cysts

'Surgery justified' is the authors' own composite, counting any neuroendocrine tumour, any solid pseudopapillary neoplasm and any symptom improvement as justification; none of these is a guideline endpoint, and the inclusion inflates the justified fraction above what any of the three guidelines was designed to achieve

115 patients spread across three guidelines, several cyst types and multiple dysplasia grades leaves nearly every subgroup in single or low double figures, and no confidence intervals accompany any accuracy estimate in the paper

19.1% of the cohort died at a median of 15 months after surgery, which bears directly on whether resection helped anyone in a cohort where 55% of operations were retrospectively unnecessary; mortality is not related to pathology, cyst type or guideline in any analysis

Because the IAP nodule criterion was relaxed - any nodule, enhancing or not, counted as a high-risk stigma because contrast was often unavailable at EUS - the IAP guideline was applied in a more inclusive form than written, which further favours it in the comparison with the AGA rule

The accuracy of preoperative diagnosis is reported as 72% overall, and 33% for serous cystic neoplasms and neuroendocrine tumours, which means the guideline comparison is being conducted on cysts whose type was frequently misidentified before the decision was made - a circularity that is described but not carried into the interpretation
The article's funding and disclosure footnotes are indicated as appearing on the last page but are not present in this text extraction, so competing interests cannot be assessed
27693645.n: 115 patients who underwent pancreatic resection for a cyst (mean age 60, SD 15.1; 57.4% female; median cyst 4.0 cm, IQR 3.0-6.1), from a database of 371 and 121 resected; IPMN was suspected in 75 of these, who formed the guideline comparison
27693645.bottom_line: Shows that all three guidelines overtreat - roughly half the resected cysts had no high-grade dysplasia or malignancy - and that the AGA rule would avoid 28% of operations at the cost of missing 12% of cysts with HGD or cancer while still performing 41% unnecessary resections; because only resected patients were studied and the cohort was selected by the IAP and European criteria, it cannot measure what any guideline misses in patients kept under surveillance, and the 12% figure rests on two lesions.

limitations: The working group did not recognise the need for major revisions, so only minor revisions were made
There is little evidence in the literature to guide the frequency and type of surveillance for IPMN

There has been no consistent data for a cut-off size of mural nodules to predict invasive carcinoma or HGD in main-duct IPMN

Cyst size is associated with increased risk but there is no cut-off to quantify it, and most of the evidence on predictors comes from retrospective surgical series, with probability rising only in the presence of more than one risk factor
Discrepant findings on the impact of surgical margin status are attributed to the retrospective nature of underpowered studies analysing small specific sub-cohorts
The Japanese twice-yearly surveillance protocol sometimes fails to detect resectable PDAC and is unlikely to be applicable globally given differences in the delivery of medical care

Nomograms are promising but warrant further validation
The precise incidence of concomitant PDAC after partial pancreatectomy has not been well documented because most reports did not discriminate it from invasive IPMN
critique: n is null, and the 31.1% and 61.6% rates that drive the branch-duct and main-duct recommendations are once again prevalences of malignancy in resected specimens; the document places them next to an observed annual progression rate of 1.4-6.9% without reconciling the two, so a reader cannot tell which number describes the patient in front of them

Cyst size is demoted as a surgical indication in the text while a 2 cm threshold is retained for patients under 65 and 3 cm remains a worrisome feature, so the criteria are internally inconsistent about the single variable the document says should not drive management

Surgical mortality and morbidity remain unquantified across the document, and the one cited study reporting overtreatment or excessive resection in 19% of cases appears as a caution rather than as an outcome that counts against the resection thresholds

All 10 authors of the revision are also authors of the 2012 version being revised and of many of the series cited, the conflict-of-interest statement is a blanket denial, and no external review, validation plan or voting procedure is described
28735806.bottom_line: A deliberately minor revision that set the enhancing mural nodule threshold at 5 mm, added CA19-9 and a growth rate above 5 mm per 2 years as worrisome features, lengthened surveillance intervals, demoted cyst size as a surgical indication, removed MCN from scope, and rejected the AGA's 5-year stopping rule in favour of indefinite surveillance; it generates no new primary evidence, reports no operating characteristics for its revised risk tiers, and its malignancy rates remain prevalences in resected series.

limitations: Absence of histological confirmation of the diagnosis of branch-duct IPMN in patients who did not undergo resection; duct communication, considered essential elsewhere, is visible on cross-sectional imaging in only a small percentage of cases
Retrospective design, so management changed over time, surveillance was not homogeneous in imaging modality or timing, and some patients were lost to follow-up

Single pancreatic referral centre, which may limit generalisability to the full population of patients with BD-IPMN; this is reflected in a median cyst size of 14 mm at diagnosis, about twice that described in radiologic series
The editor's notes add that the population size is small
critique: The 5.5% and 4.4% figures are conditional on having survived and remained under surveillance for 5 years, so the denominator of 363 is a 63% survivor subset of 577 selected for not having been resected or diagnosed with cancer earlier; the comparison 'risk may in fact be greater after 5 years (5.5% vs 4.3%)' is an artefact of unequal and non-comparable denominators rather than evidence of a rising hazard

The standardised incidence ratio of 18.8 counts high-grade dysplasia as an event while the SEER comparator counts only invasive cancer, which inflates the ratio; the authors do supply a sensitivity analysis restricted to invasive carcinoma (15.6) but the abstract and conclusions carry the 18.8

SEER rates are for the general US population rather than for people known to harbour a pancreatic cyst, so the SIR embeds the very selection it is meant to measure - a referral-centre cohort with a median 14 mm cyst is not the population from which SEER rates are drawn

The ROC analysis that produced the 1.5 cm cut-off was run on the outcome being predicted within the same 363 patients, so the 99% negative predictive value and 95% sensitivity are in-sample; no validation cohort is offered for a threshold the paper proposes as a rule

The low-risk group is defined by 5 years of stability below 1.5 cm, which cannot be known when a cyst is first found; the paper acknowledges this and still frames the cut-off as actionable, and the single event in that group was a distinct PDAC that cyst-size-based surveillance would not have prevented

118 patients (20%) were resected during follow-up, removing from the surveillance cohort exactly those cysts judged most likely to progress; the natural history reported is therefore of a cohort continuously purged of its highest-risk members

One fifth of the malignancies were anatomically distinct PDAC that cyst surveillance is not designed to detect and largely failed to detect in time (44% operable, all stage II or higher); this argues that intensifying cyst surveillance would not address a substantial share of the risk, yet the paper's recommendation is to increase rather than diminish surveillance frequency

The 'almost 8%' malignancy risk in the abstract is a whole-cohort figure that includes high-grade dysplasia found incidentally at resection, not a prospective incidence, and the 12 patients who defined the headline post-5-year risk without worrisome features had a P value of .09 against the comparison group - a non-significant difference presented as a positive finding
28739282.n: 577 patients with suspected or presumed branch-duct IPMN (median age 66, range 21-90; 59% female); median follow-up 82 months (range 6-329); 363 (63%) followed more than 5 years (median 107 months) and 121 (21%) more than 10 years (median 147 months)
28739282.bottom_line: In a referral cohort with a median follow-up of nearly 7 years, malignancy continued to appear after 5 and even 10 years and was 18.8-fold more frequent than in the US population even among patients without worrisome features at 5 years, arguing directly against the AGA's 5-year stopping rule; the figure is inflated by counting high-grade dysplasia against an invasive-cancer comparator, the denominator is restricted to five-year survivors of surveillance, and the proposed 1.5 cm low-risk threshold was fitted in the same data.

limitations: Observational design
Definitive histology and cyst morphology remain unknown; the strong T2-weighted protocol detected cysts but could not categorise worrisome features such as nodules or septal enhancement
Follow-up imaging covers only two-thirds of the baseline population, and increases in cyst number and size were frequent in that subset, so further follow-up is pending
Mid-term risk appears low but long-term risk cannot be concluded; later studies with longer intervals might reveal some cancer risk
Because baseline ran 2008-2012 and mortality follow-up ended in 2015, the mortality follow-up was only 3 years for some individuals
Only MRI was used; other modalities might add morphological features
The 2 mm detection threshold makes misinterpretation possible, and since mean cyst size was 5.20 mm with only 26 cysts over 1 cm and 3 over 2 cm, the conclusions mainly apply to small cysts
Fukuoka high-risk stigmata and worrisome features could not be assessed
Being a population-based sample, patients with pancreatic disease or prior pancreatic surgery were not excluded as they were in other studies
critique: The 49.1% headline prevalence is not an observed proportion but an estimate reweighted by two inverse-probability weights to correct for dropout from SHIP-0 to SHIP-2 and from the core examination to MRI; the observed figure was 494/1077 (45.9%), and the weighting model itself conditions on BMI, HbA1c, diabetes, lipids, smoking and income, several of which are also the exposures tested
The MRI response rate was 54.7% within a cohort already attrited from 4310 to 2333 over ten years, so the sample is at best a selected slice of the population the prevalence is claimed for

The progression denominator of 357 excludes everyone lost between SHIP-2 and SHIP-3, and those lost are nowhere characterised; if cyst carriers who died or fell ill were less likely to return, progression is underestimated by informative censoring

The claim that incidental cysts have low clinical relevance rests on zero events: there were only three pancreatic cancer deaths in 2333 people, and a 95% confidence interval around a zero numerator in cyst carriers is wide enough to include a clinically important risk - absence of evidence is reported as evidence of absence

The two participants who did die of pancreatic cancer are exactly the two who refused MRI, so the only potentially informative cases are missing from the imaging cohort, and the authors note this without allowing it to qualify the conclusion

All baseline images were read by a single observer with one year of abdominal radiology experience; the excellent kappa comes from re-reading a convenience sample of 72 of 1077 examinations with a senior reader, which bounds reproducibility but not accuracy, and there was no histological or second-modality reference standard at all

A 2 mm T2-hyperintense focus is not the lesion any guideline manages, and the paper concedes that much of what it counted is probably dysontogenetic; the recommendation of a restrictive follow-up approach for 'incidentally detected pancreatic cysts' is therefore extrapolated from lesions outside the guidelines' scope to lesions inside it

A 5-year imaging interval and a 5.9-year mortality follow-up cannot speak to a lesion whose progression to cancer is estimated to take 15-20 years; the paper's own call for a longer surveillance interval is made on a time scale shorter than the event it is meant to exclude
28877981.n: 1077 participants with analysable baseline MRCP (of 2333 in SHIP-2 and 1275 who consented to MRI); 494 harboured cysts at baseline; 676 had a 5-year follow-up MRCP; mean mortality follow-up 5.9 years (range 3.2-7.5) for the whole SHIP cohort
28877981.bottom_line: Establishes that small pancreatic cysts are extraordinarily common in the healthy general population - about half of adults on thin-slice MRCP - that they increase in number and size with age, and that over 5 years half show minimal growth; it does not establish their cancer risk, because the cohort produced no events in cyst carriers, the imaging interval was short and the lesions counted were mostly below the size any guideline manages.
28877981.funding: Deutsche Krebshilfe / Mildred-Scheel-Stiftung (109102), the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF GANI-MED 03IS2061A and BMBF 0314107, 01ZZ9603, 01ZZ0103, 01ZZ0403, 03ZIK012) and the European Union (EU-FP-7: EPC-TM); competing interests none declared

limitations: Diagnostic surgical pathology was available for only a small proportion of patients, representing a surgical selection bias
A testing selection bias exists because only specimens satisfactory for NGS and Sanger sequencing were analysed, although with a 7% failure rate the effect is likely minimal
The follow-up period is relatively short to assess the clinical impact of detecting TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN or AKT1 alterations; monitoring is planned to continue

The panel omitted RNF43, CDKN2A and SMAD4; RNF43 might improve MCN detection but has only an 8-35% prevalence in MCN, and CDKN2A and SMAD4 deletions are associated with high-grade dysplasia and adenocarcinoma
Additional studies are required to identify the minimal gene set needed
The study does not address how to integrate DNA-based testing into current surveillance protocols
Assessment of MCNs using KRAS is a notable limitation, as is the use of Sanger sequencing for pancreatic cyst evaluation
critique: The allele-frequency rules that produce 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity were derived by inspecting the same 102 resected cases on which they are then scored, and the GNAS >55% rule rests on exactly two cysts; the pre-specified gene combination gave 79-88% sensitivity, so the headline perfect performance is a fitted result reported alongside an unfitted comparator

Verification is severely partial - 102 of 595 patients (17%) - and resection was driven by Fukuoka features together with the molecular result itself, so the comparator tests (duct dilatation, mural nodule, cytology) helped determine who entered the denominator; this depresses their measured sensitivity by the same mechanism that inflates NGS

Advanced neoplasia was present in 19 of 102 resected patients but at an unknown and far lower rate in the 493 who were not resected, so the positive predictive values implied here do not transfer to a surveillance clinic

The 30% KRAS sensitivity for MCN is folded into a headline of 89% for 'mucinous cysts' because IPMNs outnumbered MCNs 56 to 10; a clinician applying the test to a body-or-tail cyst in a middle-aged woman faces the 30% figure, not the 89%

'All 16 patients are alive and well and have not developed pancreatic cancer' is offered as reassurance about low-level TP53/PIK3CA/PTEN mutations, but the median follow-up is 26 months for a lesion whose progression takes years, so the statement has no discriminating power

One cyst lost its TP53 mutation between aspirations and three of 16 Sanger-negative cysts became NGS-positive on retesting; reproducibility is therefore a function of sampling adequacy, yet no repeat-testing concordance statistic is given for the panel as a whole

The assay is the authors' own clinical test, charged at $750, and the paper functions in part as its validation and promotion; no comparison is made with the cost of the imaging or surgery it is meant to avert

Sanger sequencing is used as the comparator for the sensitivity argument but also as the sole method for VHL, so the paper simultaneously discourages Sanger and reports VHL prevalence by it, conceding that the 8% figure is likely inaccurate
28970292.n: 673 EUS-FNA cyst fluid specimens from 642 patients, of which 626 specimens from 595 patients were satisfactory; surgical pathology in 102 patients (17%); separate Sanger cohort of 175 cysts from 169 patients, 159 satisfactory, 34 with diagnostic pathology
28970292.bottom_line: Establishes in a large prospective single-centre series that deep NGS of preoperative cyst fluid is 100% sensitive for IPMN and 100% specific for a mucinous cyst, far more sensitive than Sanger sequencing, and that TP53/PIK3CA/PTEN alterations mark advanced neoplasia better than duct dilatation, mural nodules or cytology; the 100% figures for advanced neoplasia depend on allele-frequency rules fitted to the same 102 resected cases, and only 17% of the cohort was verified.
28970292.funding: Supported in part by grants from the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network (Translational Research Grant), the National Pancreas Foundation Western Pennsylvania Chapter and the University of Pittsburgh (to AD Singhi); competing interests none declared

limitations: The quality of evidence on which the recommendations are based is poor; the guideline grades all 20 recommendations as low or very low quality and calls for prospective multicentre studies
There are very little data to evaluate whether surveillance intervals can be extended, or whether surveillance should be discontinued if cysts are stable after a specified time period

There are no studies to guide the decision of when to stop surveillance of pancreatic cysts by age, nor are cost-effectiveness analyses available to estimate the cost-benefit ratio of surveillance in an elderly population; the age-75 recommendation is explicitly stated to have no evidence supporting it

Conflicting results exist on the risk of high-grade dysplasia or cancer after resection of IPMN with low- or intermediate-grade dysplasia, and there is insufficient evidence to support no surveillance in that group
Insufficient evidence exists to recommend routine use of molecular markers, cyst ablation, or needle microbiopsy forceps
The management algorithms do not address every possible clinical scenario, so management must be tailored to the individual patient
Attributing symptoms to a cyst may be very difficult in the case of non-specific abdominal symptoms, and abdominal pain is usually not attributable to the cyst even when it prompted the imaging
Large, prospective, multicentre studies following presumed mucinous cysts are required to answer the critical question of the cumulative risk of high-grade dysplasia or cancer
critique: n is null and the guideline sets its own two evidence streams in opposition without resolving them: a 0.24% per year transformation risk computed by assuming all pancreatic cancer arises in cysts, and a 42% high-grade-dysplasia-or-cancer rate in 9,249 resected IPMNs. The reassurance in the introduction comes from the first and the surveillance schedule from the second

The surveillance algorithm - four years of biennial MRI under 1 cm, three years of annual MRI for 1-2 cm, alternating 6-monthly MRI and EUS above 3 cm - is presented as a detailed figure with no evidence cited for any specific interval or endpoint, which is precisely the criticism the document levels at the AGA's 1-then-2-year schedule

The age cut-offs of 75 and 85 are transplanted from USPSTF colorectal cancer screening with the authors' own acknowledgement that no evidence supports them; borrowing an age limit from a disease with a validated screening test, a different natural history and a different intervention is a category error that the guideline names and then acts on anyway

Growth of more than 3 mm per year is adopted as a high-risk characteristic with no operating characteristics cited, and the AGA technical review the guideline otherwise draws on had found that an increase in cyst size was not a statistically significant risk factor for malignancy

The AGA stopping rule is rejected on the strength of case-level observations - cancers appearing up to 16 years out, and genetic estimates of a 15-20 year dwell time - rather than an incidence estimate, so the decision to continue indefinite surveillance in fit patients is taken with no calculation of how many cancers that policy would catch, at what cost, or against what competing mortality; the guideline states that no cost-effectiveness analysis exists and does not attempt one

Cyst fluid CEA is recommended for distinguishing cyst type at a sensitivity the guideline itself reports as 63%, and cytology for detecting high-grade dysplasia at a sensitivity of 65%; both are endorsed as 'may be considered' without any statement of what a negative result licenses, which is the question a clinician actually faces

The strong recommendation that resected MCN without cancer needs no surveillance rests on a 90-patient series and a 344-patient review in which no MCN under 3 cm with a normal CA19-9 and no concerning features harboured high-grade dysplasia or cancer - an absence of events in modest series, graded low quality, yet given a strong recommendation

Excluding patients with a family history or germline mutation removes from scope the group in whom surveillance is most likely to be worthwhile, leaving the general gastroenterologist the guideline is written for without guidance for exactly the patients who most need an individualised plan

The comorbidity evidence invoked to justify not evaluating unfit patients (78% of deaths unrelated to the IPMN; an 11-fold higher non-IPMN death rate at a Charlson-age index of 7 or more) argues equally against indefinite surveillance in fit elderly patients, but is applied only to the first conclusion
29485131.bottom_line: The ACG guideline supplies a practical, size-stratified surveillance algorithm, explicitly refuses the AGA's 5-year stopping rule in surgically fit patients, and introduces age 75 as the point to reconsider surveillance; all 20 recommendations are graded low or very low quality, the intervals and the age limits are acknowledged to be unsupported by evidence, and patients with a family history or predisposing mutation are outside its scope.
29485131.funding: Supported by the American College of Gastroenterology; potential competing interests: none. Guarantor of the article: Grace H. Elta

limitations: The recommendations are predominantly graded 2C, and several key statements - the main duct >5 mm resection threshold, pancreatoscopy and nCLE - achieved only weak agreement among the expert panel

The accuracy of imaging for identifying the specific type of pancreatic cystic neoplasm remains relatively low whether single or combined modalities are used, including for differentiating small lesions from non-neoplastic or non-epithelial cysts and for duct communication
Data on EUS-based differentiation between benign and malignant lesions are conflicting, and there is considerable interobserver variation in EUS-based diagnoses
The role of EUS-FNA in diagnosis is still a matter of debate and consensus in the literature is lacking
The minimal versus extensive main-duct involvement classification can be used only after resection and is thus irrelevant to preoperative clinical assessment
No definite MRI or CT protocol can be recommended because of the wide spread of published data and the lack of dedicated comparative studies
There are conflicting data and opinions about the extent of surgery for main-duct IPMN; few studies have investigated mixed-type IPMN as a single entity

Earlier studies evaluated features associated with malignant transformation for all mucinous lesions combined, whereas IPMN and MCN may differ in growth rate, transformation risk and predictive features
critique: n is null and the malignancy rates that set every threshold are prevalences in resected specimens: the tabulated 30-91% for main duct dilatation comes from five retrospective surgical series of 52-320 patients, so lowering the resection threshold to more than 5 mm is a decision derived from the composition of past operations rather than from the outcome of observing such ducts

The headline divergence from the IAP guidelines - a 40 mm rather than 30 mm size threshold for conservative management - is adopted with no head-to-head comparison, and the surrounding text simultaneously reports that cysts of 30 mm or more carry a 12-47% malignancy risk and that a cyst under 30 mm growing more than 2 mm per year carries a 45% five-year risk; the 40 mm line cannot be reconciled with the evidence printed beside it

The main duct >5 mm resection threshold carried only weak agreement among the guideline's own experts and is graded 2C, yet it is set out as a recommendation on the same footing as 1B statements; the voting result is reported but its implication for how much confidence the reader should place in that statement is never discussed

GRADE labels are applied inconsistently: several statements that no useful evidence exists are graded 1B, which in GRADE denotes high-quality evidence supporting a strong recommendation, so the grades cannot be taken at face value and the 'evidence-based' framing of the title is not borne out by the ratings

nCLE is recommended against at GRADE 1C on the strength of an adverse event rate and two citations - a strong recommendation on thin evidence, and in the opposite direction from the caution the document exercises elsewhere

Lifelong surveillance until the patient is unfit for surgery is recommended at GRADE 1B with no estimate of cancers prevented, no competing-risk analysis in a seventh-decade population and no cost analysis; the single comorbidity study cited in support reports that patients with a Charlson-age index of 7 or more have an 11-fold risk of comorbidity-related death within 3 years and only 6% die of malignant IPMN, which is evidence against the recommendation it accompanies
Surgical mortality and morbidity are nowhere pooled or stated anywhere in the document, so not one of its surgical recommendations is accompanied by the risk of acting on it

The guideline covers all cyst types while reporting its own accuracy for identifying the specific type as 40-95%, so type-specific thresholds are applied to a diagnosis that is wrong a substantial fraction of the time; the circularity is described in the radiology section and never carried into the recommendations

The statement that SCN specific mortality is nearly zero and that cases reported as malignant 'do not fulfil the WHO criteria' makes the entity benign partly by definition, and the recommendation to stop following a confirmed SCN after one year rests on that definitional move plus two cohort studies
29574408.bottom_line: The European guideline widened scope to all pancreatic cystic neoplasms, set a 40 mm size threshold for conservative management, lowered the main-duct resection threshold to more than 5 mm, released confirmed serous cystic neoplasms from surveillance after a year, and mandated lifelong follow-up while a patient remains fit for surgery; despite the evidence-based framing most statements are GRADE 2C, several key ones achieved only weak expert agreement, no surgical risk is quantified anywhere, and its malignancy thresholds come from retrospective resected series.
29574408.funding: The authors have not declared a specific grant for this research from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors; competing interests none declared

limitations: Data came from a single tertiary referral centre, potentially producing referral bias

The incidence of pancreatic carcinoma appeared higher than estimated from the prevalence of pancreatic cysts and the incidence of pancreatic cancer in the general Japanese population, and the branch-duct IPMNs were larger than reported for incidentally diagnosed lesions
A vast majority of the population was Japanese, so the data should be validated in independent populations

Molecular analyses were not available for all patients who developed pancreatic carcinoma, and in GNAS-wild-type carcinomas further analyses beyond KRAS might be required for a definite conclusion on derived versus concomitant origin
The small number of high-grade dysplasia cases (7) precluded robust statistical assessment of that subgroup
critique: The cohort excluded mural nodules and MPD >=10 mm at baseline and then counts later-appearing mural nodules and carcinomas as outcomes, and it excluded anyone diagnosed with cancer or resected within 6 months; that 6-month window removes prevalent disease from the numerator while retaining its risk factors in the denominator, which is immortal time and biases the incidence estimate downward early and the hazard ratios upward

The three nested denominators - 1404, then 804, then 737 - are progressively enriched survivor sets, and the AGA-criteria subgroup is constructed retrospectively using information from the first 5 years; the AGA rule would be applied prospectively, so 'patients in whom the AGA would stop surveillance' is not the group the AGA rule actually identifies

The SIR comparator is the age- and sex-matched Japanese population, of whom some 2-7% also harbour a pancreatic cyst, so part of the 10.8-fold excess is detection rather than incidence; the authors note that their own incidence exceeds what cyst prevalence and population cancer rates would predict, which is the same objection seen from the inside
High-grade dysplasia (7 of 38 derived carcinomas) is counted as an event against a registry denominator that counts only invasive cancer, inflating every SIR in the paper

The derived-versus-concomitant distinction that carries the paper's main biological claim was adjudicated molecularly in only 13 of 68 cases and radiologically or histologically in the rest; a GNAS mutation alone was taken as sufficient to call a carcinoma IPMN-derived, and the one case where this overturned the pathological reading is presented as validation of the method rather than as a measure of its uncertainty

Nearly half the carcinomas (30 of 68, and 14 of 30 after 5 years) were concomitant PDAC, whose incidence was unrelated to any IPMN feature except age; the paper's recommendation to continue surveillance therefore rests substantially on a risk that its own risk factors cannot stratify and that imaging of the cyst is not designed to detect

In a centre where the whole resected pancreas is sliced at 5 mm and clinicians are primed to look for concomitant PDAC, both the ascertainment of that entity and its apparent frequency are higher than they would be elsewhere; this makes the Japanese concomitant-PDAC literature and the global recommendation drawn from it hard to separate

Postoperative morbidity was 75% with major morbidity in 26% among the 57 resected, and 19 of those 57 had only low-grade dysplasia - the cost of the surveillance-and-resection strategy the paper advocates is reported but never set against the incidence figures it is recommending be acted upon
31473224.n: 1404 consecutive patients with branch-duct IPMN (52% women, mean age 67.5 years, median IPMN 14 mm), 9231 person-years, median follow-up 6.0 years (range 0.5-21.8); 804 (57%) analysed after 5-year surveillance (3598 person-years, median 3.9 further years); subgroups of 732 with IPMN <15 mm, 1335 with MPD <5 mm, and 737 meeting AGA criteria for discontinuation
31473224.bottom_line: The largest single-centre long-term branch-duct IPMN series shows pancreatic carcinoma incidence rising to 15% at 15 years, a tenfold excess over the matched population, and a risk that persists past 5 years even in cysts under 15 mm with a non-dilated duct - arguing against the AGA stopping rule; it does not establish that continued surveillance changes outcome, and roughly half the cancers were concomitant PDACs that no IPMN feature predicted.
31473224.funding: No funding statement; conflicts of interest: the authors disclose no conflicts

limitations: No studies at all exist on prophylactic total pancreatectomy, so the decision tables necessarily rest on indirect evidence
Evidence on minimally invasive total pancreatectomy is poorly described in the literature, from only 35 patients in 7 studies, with short follow-up of 3-38 months in a prior review
Individuals with familial clustering were excluded because the exact pancreatic cancer risk is unknown, with wide confidence intervals
The relative roles of CFTR and SPINK1 mutations in carcinogenesis are not as well established as PRSS1, so those patients were excluded from this first programme
The programme explicitly does not aim to lower the threshold for prophylactic total pancreatectomy
For patients with IPMN there could be a considerable risk of misdiagnosis of approximately 20%
It remains unclear whether screening programmes improve survival in high-risk individuals; no randomised controlled trials exist and the only data are prospective cohorts

Glucose control after total pancreatectomy may be challenging because of complete loss of both insulin and glucagon secretion, predisposing to difficult hypo- and hyperglycaemia; a recent systematic review found a need for further improvement in diabetes management, especially prevention of hypoglycaemia-related morbidity and mortality
critique: The decision tables tell patients that 2-5 of 100 will die from the operation in very high-volume centres, while the review's own pooled 30-day mortality across 3570 patients was 6% (95% CI 4-8%); the figure given to patients is lower than the figure the authors generated, and the substitution is never justified in the text

The 60% cancer risk on the other side of the table is taken from Salvia's resected main-duct series - the prevalence of malignancy in operated specimens - not a lifetime incidence in surveilled patients; the two sides of the comparison are therefore measured on incompatible scales, and the comparison that drives the whole programme systematically overstates the benefit

The programme is built on minimally invasive total pancreatectomy, whose entire evidence base here is 35 patients in seven small series with a reported 0% mortality - a figure no sample of that size could detect, since the upper 95% bound on zero deaths in 35 patients is about 10%

The pooled total pancreatectomy outcomes mix indications - malignancy, chronic pancreatitis, IPMN - without separating them, although the prophylactic candidate is a well patient who will tolerate complications differently from one operated for cancer

Quality of life is described as 'slightly' or 'moderately' lower from 102 patients in 4 studies, with no comparison against the surveillance alternative and no utility weighting, so the table cannot support the trade-off it asks patients to make

No decision analysis, Markov model, life-expectancy calculation or cost analysis underlies tables intended to guide an irreversible operation with 100% insulin-dependent diabetes as its certain consequence

The authors report that 97 international experts split 41/59 on the very indication the tables encode, and that in elderly patients with main-duct IPMN with worrisome features disease-specific 5-year survival without surgery was 81%; both facts argue that the European guideline advice the programme implements is unsettled, yet the tables present the surveillance arm's risk as a settled 60%

Crino et al. contributes a 61 of 61 (100%) diagnostic yield and an 18% bleeding rate - an outlier in both directions - and drives both the yield estimate and the adverse event estimate without a sensitivity analysis excluding it

The reference standard includes 'consensus between experts' and 'cyst fluid analysis', which means the index test can inform the truth it is being judged against; the authors exclude CEA-only reference standards for this reason but then permit consensus and cyst fluid criteria, which has the same circularity

The headline conclusion of 'excellent diagnostic accuracy' is asserted for a specificity point estimate of 88% that sits on I2 = 79%; with that much between-study variation a single pooled specificity is not a meaningful quantity, and the abstract does not carry the caveat

Studies using cutoffs of 30, 41 and 50 mg/dL were pooled into one 'low glucose' estimate, which assumes threshold-invariance; the authors state the ideal threshold is unknown, so the pooled figure describes no implementable test
Two of seven studies were conference abstracts, and one of these (Rossi, cutoff 30 mg/dL) contributes the only 100% specificity in the set

A pooled sensitivity of 90.5% with I2 = 0% across studies using different cutoffs, different assays and different reference standards is implausibly homogeneous and is more likely to reflect small numbers of mucinous cases per study than a stable biological threshold

The glucometer subgroup - the most clinically attractive version of the test, and the one named in the conclusion - rests on three studies and has the lowest specificity (83.9%) and widest interval (68.5-92.6) of any subgroup

limitations: Multiple thresholds and cutoffs for glucose and multiple measurement modalities were pooled, although sensitivity analyses, subgroup analyses and univariable meta-regression did not identify variable cutoffs as a source of between-study heterogeneity

No diagnostic algorithms yet exist for integrating glucose into practice and no study has addressed that clinically relevant question
critique: The reference standard is the central problem and is only half-acknowledged: in most contributing studies non-mucinous cysts were never resected and were classified using the same imaging and cyst fluid criteria the index test is being compared against, which is incorporation bias and inflates both sensitivity and specificity in the same direction
Three of the eight studies were conference abstracts, not peer reviewed, and several supplied only the 2x2 table, so study-level quality could not be properly appraised despite the QUADAS-2 exercise
